question: Contoso Logistics routes 4.2 million support emails a month through a triage step that assigns one of eight intent labels and pulls out the tracking number. The step runs on a Global Standard gpt-4.1 deployment, costs roughly $38,000 a month, and shows p95 latency of 2.1 seconds against a 96.4% accuracy score on a labelled holdout set. The team wants the cost and latency down without losing measurable accuracy. Which change should they evaluate first?
options: Deploy a small language model such as Phi-4-mini from the Foundry model catalog, score it against the same labelled holdout set, and fall back to gpt-4.1 only for low-confidence messages
Keep the gpt-4.1 deployment but reduce max_tokens and set temperature to 0 so each triage call consumes fewer tokens and returns faster
Fine-tune gpt-4.1 on 50,000 historical triage emails so the fine-tuned model needs shorter prompts and produces the labels more cheaply
Switch the triage step to a reasoning model so the extra deliberation raises accuracy enough to justify the current spend
optionExplanations: Correct. Fixed-taxonomy classification plus one short extraction is exactly the workload a small language model handles at a fraction of the cost and latency of a frontier model, and the labelled holdout set already exists so the accuracy claim can be measured rather than assumed. Routing only low-confidence items to gpt-4.1 preserves the tail quality while moving the bulk of 4.2 million calls to the cheap model.

Tempting because token settings do affect cost, but this workload emits a label and a tracking number — the output is already tiny, so the bill is dominated by input tokens and per-call model pricing. Trimming max_tokens shaves a rounding error off a $38,000 invoice and does nothing about per-token input price on a frontier model.

Fine-tuning does shorten prompts, but it keeps you on the expensive model family, adds hosting charges for the fine-tuned deployment, and locks in a training-time snapshot of the intent taxonomy that has to be retrained whenever labels change. For a simple eight-class problem, a smaller base model is cheaper to run and far cheaper to maintain.

Reasoning models spend extra internal tokens on deliberation, which raises both cost and latency — the opposite of the stated goal. They pay off on multi-step planning or hard analytical problems, not on a single-pass classification task that is already at 96.4%.
principle: match model size to task difficulty, then prove it on your own eval set
relatedConcept: The Foundry model catalog spans frontier LLMs, small language models, and multimodal models precisely so each step of a pipeline can run on the cheapest model that clears its quality bar.
overallExplanation: High-volume, narrow tasks like fixed-label classification belong on a small language model, with a confidence-based fallback to a larger model for the hard tail. Always validate the swap against the labelled holdout set you already have instead of arguing about it.

question: A claims processor receives about 30,000 scanned repair invoices a day in mixed formats: printed line items, handwritten adjuster notes in the margin, and photographs of damaged parts stapled to the page. Downstream systems need a consistent JSON record with vendor, line items, totals, and a description of the visible damage. Which Foundry approach fits the requirement best?
options: Configure an Azure Content Understanding analyzer that defines the target fields once and processes the document and image content into structured JSON for every invoice
Send each page as an image to a chat completion call with a prompt asking for the fields as JSON, and parse whatever the model returns
Run the pages through an OCR-only text extraction step and pass the raw text to a small language model for field extraction
Fine-tune a multimodal model on 5,000 labelled invoices so it learns the specific layouts used by the top vendors

Content Understanding is the Foundry Tool built for multimodal extraction: you declare a field schema in an analyzer and it combines OCR, layout, and visual understanding to return the same structured JSON for every input, including handwriting and attached photos. Declaring the schema once is what makes 30,000 documents a day predictable instead of prompt-by-prompt guesswork.

Freeform prompting a chat model can work for a demo, but it gives no schema contract, so field names and types drift between calls and parsing failures surface only downstream. It also ignores layout signals that a purpose-built analyzer uses to keep line items aligned with their totals.

OCR-only extraction throws away exactly the information that makes this case hard: handwritten margin notes read poorly as flat text and the damage photographs contain no text at all. A text-only pipeline cannot produce the visual damage description the requirement calls for.

Fine-tuning is heavy machinery for a problem the platform already solves declaratively, and a layout-specific fine-tune degrades the moment a vendor changes its invoice template. It also does nothing to guarantee schema-valid output, which is the actual downstream requirement.
principle: declarative extraction schemas beat freeform prompts for repeatable document workloads
relatedConcept: Foundry Tools such as Content Understanding cover multimodal document, image, audio, and video extraction so teams do not hand-build OCR plus prompt pipelines for every format.
overallExplanation: Mixed print, handwriting, and photo content that must land in a fixed JSON shape is the Content Understanding analyzer scenario. Declaring fields once gives schema stability across 30,000 documents a day that ad-hoc prompting cannot.

On a GPT-4.1 deployment the assistant reaches the right verdict on 71% of the 200-case regression suite, usually failing when the exclusions interact. Latency of up to 30 seconds per case is acceptable. What is the most appropriate model choice?
options: Deploy a reasoning model from the model catalog for the eligibility step and keep the cheaper chat model for summarizing the final decision for the customer
Keep GPT-4.1 and raise temperature to 0.9 so the model explores more interpretations of the interacting exclusions
Keep GPT-4.1 and add the phrase asking it to think step by step to the system prompt, since that produces the same deliberation as a reasoning model
Move the eligibility step to a small language model and pass the exclusions matrix as a longer, more explicit prompt
optionExplanations: Correct. Multi-document deduction with interacting rules is the workload reasoning models are trained for, and the 30-second latency budget makes their extra deliberation affordable. Splitting the pipeline keeps the expensive model on the hard step while a cheap chat model handles the plain-language write-up.

Higher temperature increases sampling randomness, not analytical depth. On a rules-and-exclusions problem it makes the verdict less reproducible across runs, which is the opposite of what an underwriting audit trail needs.

Prompted step-by-step text helps a little, but it is surface-level narration produced by the same model that is already failing on interacting exclusions. A reasoning model allocates real inference-time compute to the deduction, which prompt wording cannot manufacture.

Going smaller on the hardest step in the pipeline trades away exactly the capability the failures point to. Longer prompts add context but do not give a small model the deductive depth to resolve interacting exclusions.
principle: spend inference-time reasoning only where the deduction is genuinely hard
relatedConcept: Choosing a model per task means mixing families inside one solution — reasoning models for planning and deduction, standard chat models for drafting and summarizing.
overallExplanation: Interacting-rule deduction with a generous latency budget is the canonical reasoning-model case; temperature and step-by-step prompt wording do not substitute for inference-time reasoning. Keep the cheap chat model for the presentation step.

question: A contact centre wants agents in Manila to take live calls from Spanish-speaking customers. The requirement is that the customer's speech is rendered as Spanish text and English audio with under two seconds of lag while the caller is still speaking, and that a transcript in both languages is stored for QA. Which Foundry capability should anchor the design?
options: Azure AI Speech in Foundry Tools, using continuous speech translation with streaming recognition and text to speech for the rendered audio
A multimodal chat model called once per completed call with the recorded audio file attached and a prompt asking for a translated transcript
Azure AI Translator called on the final call transcript after the call ends, with the translated text played back to the agent afterwards
A custom function tool on an agent that uploads 30-second audio chunks to blob storage and polls a batch transcription job
optionExplanations: Correct. Speech translation in Azure AI Speech is designed for streaming audio: it recognizes and translates continuously while the speaker talks and emits partial results, which is what keeps lag inside two seconds, and text to speech renders the English audio. The service returns both recognized and translated text, so the bilingual QA transcript falls out of the same pipeline.

A single post-call multimodal call cannot help a live conversation at all — the translation arrives after the customer has hung up. Batch multimodal audio analysis is a good fit for QA scoring, not for in-call assistance.

Translator handles text well, but it starts from text that does not exist yet during a live call and this design explicitly defers playback until the call ends. It solves the transcript requirement while missing the latency requirement entirely.

Chunk upload plus batch transcription polling adds storage round trips and job scheduling delay measured in tens of seconds. Batch transcription targets recorded archives, not the sub-two-second interactive path.
principle: real-time modality requirements pick the service before the model does
relatedConcept: Foundry Tools include purpose-built speech, translation, and vision services; a generative model is the wrong tool when the hard requirement is streaming latency.
overallExplanation: Live bilingual calls need streaming speech translation plus text to speech, not post-call batch processing. Latency requirements, not model capability, are what disqualify the batch-shaped options here.

question: A benefits helpdesk assistant must answer from roughly 400 HR policy documents. Policies are revised every week by the HR team, answers must quote the exact clause and link to the source document, and an incorrect quotation is treated as a compliance incident. The team is debating how to give the model this knowledge. Which approach fits the constraints?
options: Index the documents in Azure AI Search and ground each answer with retrieved passages, returning the document link and clause as citations with the response
Fine-tune a chat model on the policy corpus each month so the knowledge is carried in the model weights and no retrieval hop is needed
Paste the full policy corpus into the system prompt of a long-context model so every answer sees all 400 documents
Store the policies as few-shot examples in the prompt template, refreshing the examples whenever HR publishes a revision
optionExplanations: Correct. Retrieval keeps the knowledge outside the model, so a weekly policy revision is an index update rather than a model change, and the retrieved passage is the natural source of a verbatim clause plus its document link. Grounding on retrieved text is also what makes the citation checkable, which is the compliance requirement.

Fine-tuning teaches style and format far better than it teaches facts, and a monthly cycle guarantees the model is stale for up to four weeks against weekly revisions. Worse, weights carry no citation, so there is nothing to link a quoted clause back to.

Even where the context window physically fits, sending 400 documents on every question is enormously expensive per call, pushes latency up, and dilutes attention across mostly irrelevant policy text. It also gives no retrieval score to justify which clause was used.

Few-shot examples shape output format; they are not a knowledge store, and a handful of examples cannot represent 400 documents. This conflates demonstrating an answer style with providing the source material an answer must be grounded in.
principle: frequently changing, citable knowledge belongs in an index, not in weights
relatedConcept: Choosing a grounding service is a separate decision from choosing a model: Azure AI Search supplies the passages, the model supplies the wording.
overallExplanation: Weekly-changing policies that must be quoted and linked are a retrieval-grounding problem. Fine-tuning and prompt-stuffing both fail the freshness and citation constraints that define this scenario.

Register the equipment status API with the agent as an OpenAPI specified tool so the agent can call its operations directly
Copy the maintenance PDFs into the agent instructions as background context so no retrieval service is required
Write a single custom function tool that proxies all 40 API operations behind one action parameter the model must fill in

relatedConcept: Agent solutions assemble knowledge, memory, and tool integrations; Foundry supplies search-backed knowledge tools and OpenAPI tool import so each is configuration rather than custom plumbing.

question: A parts-lookup assistant retrieves from an Azure AI Search index using pure vector search over embedded product descriptions. Users report that natural-language questions work well, but queries containing exact identifiers such as BRK-4471-A or ISO 4762 return semantically similar parts and almost never the exact one. Recall on the identifier subset of the evaluation set is 0.41. What should you change in the retrieval design?
options: Switch to hybrid retrieval that runs keyword and vector queries together and fuses the result sets, then apply the semantic ranker to reorder the top results
Increase k from 5 to 50 so the exact part is more likely to appear somewhere in the retrieved set
Re-embed the corpus with a larger embedding model and more dimensions so identifiers are represented more precisely
Lower the vector similarity threshold so borderline matches are no longer filtered out of the result set
optionExplanations: Correct. Embeddings capture meaning, not exact token identity, so rare alphanumeric identifiers are systematically weak in vector space — the keyword arm of a hybrid query matches them lexically, and fusing the two result sets recovers the exact document. Adding the semantic ranker then reorders the fused candidates so the exact match surfaces at the top rather than merely being present.

Widening k is a blunt instrument: it inflates prompt size and cost, and it only helps if the exact document was ranked just below the cutoff. Here the vector representation of an identifier is weak in the first place, so the right document often is not in the top 50 either.

Larger embedding models improve semantic nuance, not lexical exactness. A rare SKU token is still diluted into a dense vector regardless of dimension count, so this spends compute and index storage for essentially no gain on the failing subset.

Loosening the threshold returns more marginally similar parts — precisely the wrong parts users are already complaining about. It treats a representation mismatch as if it were an over-aggressive filter.
principle: identifiers need lexical matching; meaning needs vectors; production needs both
relatedConcept: Choosing a retrieval method means matching query shape to search mode — keyword, vector, or hybrid with semantic reranking — rather than defaulting to vectors everywhere.
overallExplanation: Exact-identifier queries fail in pure vector search because embeddings encode meaning, not tokens. Hybrid retrieval with fused keyword and vector results plus the semantic ranker is the standard fix.

question: A media company keeps 2.1 million documents in Azure Blob Storage; about 9,000 are added or edited each day. They need a searchable vector index kept close to current, and the platform team wants as little bespoke pipeline code as possible. Which indexing approach should they choose?
options: Configure an Azure AI Search indexer with a skillset that performs integrated vectorization on a schedule, relying on change tracking to process only new and modified blobs
Write a nightly job that reads every blob, calls the embeddings deployment for each document, and pushes the full corpus to the index with the push API
Have the application embed and upload each document at query time so the index is only populated for content users actually ask about
Store the documents as agent knowledge files and let the agent re-read the blob container on each run instead of maintaining an index
optionExplanations: Correct. An indexer with a skillset gives you chunking and integrated vectorization inside Azure AI Search, and blob change tracking means each scheduled run touches only the roughly 9,000 changed documents rather than all 2.1 million. That is both the cheapest incremental path and the least custom code to own.

A full nightly re-embed of 2.1 million documents burns embedding tokens on unchanged content every single night and takes a long maintenance window. The push API is the right choice when you need custom transforms, not when the platform already offers change-tracked incremental indexing.

Embedding at query time means the first user to ask about a document gets a miss, so the index is permanently incomplete and recall depends on query history. It also puts embedding latency directly on the user's request path.

Re-reading a 2.1 million document container on every agent run is not a retrieval strategy — there is no ranking, no incremental update, and enormous per-run cost. Knowledge files suit small curated sets, not a corpus of this size.
principle: prefer change-tracked incremental indexing over full re-processing
relatedConcept: Indexing method selection covers who chunks and embeds the content: an indexer with integrated vectorization, or a custom push pipeline you build and operate yourself.
overallExplanation: Large corpora with a small daily delta call for an Azure AI Search indexer plus skillset with integrated vectorization and change tracking. Nightly full re-embeds and query-time indexing both pay repeatedly for work already done.

question: A retail search index holds 48 million chunks with 3,072-dimension float32 embeddings. The search service is close to its storage quota, monthly cost is the main complaint, and the team has confirmed that a small drop in top-10 ranking quality is acceptable as long as the final results stay accurate. Which change addresses the cost pressure most directly?
options: Enable vector compression with quantization on the index and configure oversampling with rescoring against the original vectors
Reduce the number of documents in the index by dropping every chunk that has not been returned in a query in the last 90 days
Switch the vector profile from an HNSW algorithm to exhaustive KNN so no graph structure has to be stored
Move the vector fields into a second search service so the storage is spread across two quotas
optionExplanations: Correct. Quantization compresses each vector to a much smaller representation, which is the dominant storage cost at 48 million by 3,072 dimensions, and oversampling with rescoring against the retained full-precision vectors recovers most of the ranking quality lost to compression. That trade is exactly the one the team already agreed to accept.

Pruning by recent query history silently deletes long-tail content, so questions about it become unanswerable rather than merely lower-ranked. It also attacks document count when the real driver is bytes per vector.

Exhaustive KNN removes the ANN graph but scans every vector at query time, so latency scales linearly with a 48 million document index. It trades a modest storage saving for a serious query-performance regression.

Splitting fields across two services multiplies fixed service cost, forces the application to merge results from two systems, and does nothing to reduce total bytes stored. It relabels the quota problem instead of solving it.
principle: shrink the vectors before you shrink the corpus
relatedConcept: Retrieval design decisions include index-level storage settings — vector dimensions, compression, and oversampling — not just which search mode to query with.
overallExplanation: Vector storage cost at scale is addressed with quantization plus oversampling and rescoring, which preserves most ranking quality. Deleting content, disabling ANN, or splitting services all trade away more than they save.

question: A travel agent built on Foundry Agent Service currently keeps conversation state in the web tier: the app stores every user and assistant message in its own session cache and replays the whole transcript into a new run each turn. After a deployment that scaled the web tier to three replicas, users behind the load balancer intermittently see the agent forget what was just said. What should the team change?
options: Use Agent Service threads as the conversation store, creating a thread per conversation and adding each new user message to that thread before starting a run
Enable sticky sessions on the load balancer so every request from a user lands on the replica holding that user's cache
Increase the session cache TTL in the web tier and raise the number of messages retained per session
Move the transcript into the agent instructions before each run so the conversation history travels with the agent definition
optionExplanations: Correct. Agent Service threads are server-side, durable conversation state: the thread holds the message history and each run reads it, so any replica can continue the conversation by referencing the thread id. That removes the per-replica cache that the scale-out just exposed as the real bug.

Sticky sessions hide the symptom by pinning users to a replica, but the state is still confined to a single process — a replica restart, rebalance, or deployment loses the conversation. It also undermines even load distribution across the three replicas.

TTL and retention tuning make the in-process cache hold more for longer, which does nothing about the fact that a different replica has no copy at all. This treats an eviction problem that is not happening.

Agent instructions define role and behaviour and are not a per-conversation store; rewriting them per run mutates shared agent configuration and would leak one user's transcript into another's session. Conversation history belongs on the thread, not the agent.
principle: conversation memory belongs in durable server-side threads, not in app process state
relatedConcept: Choosing memory integration for agents means deciding where conversation state lives — Agent Service threads give a managed, run-aware store that survives scale-out.
overallExplanation: Server-side threads make conversation state independent of which replica serves a request, which is exactly what breaks when app-tier caches meet horizontal scale. Sticky sessions and bigger caches only postpone the same failure.

question: A legal knowledge agent must serve four practice groups from one corpus of 180,000 documents. Each document carries a group access list, and a user must never receive content from a group they do not belong to — not even as a summary. The team is choosing between agent file search over uploaded files and an Azure AI Search connection. Which design satisfies the access requirement?
options: Index the documents in Azure AI Search with a group field, and have the application pass the caller's groups as a search filter on every retrieval so restricted documents are never returned
Upload all 180,000 documents to a single agent file search store and add an instruction telling the agent to ignore documents the user is not entitled to see
Upload the documents to file search and post-process the model's answer, removing any sentence that cites a document outside the caller's groups
Index everything in Azure AI Search without an access field and rely on a content filter policy to block responses that contain restricted material
optionExplanations: Correct. Security trimming works by never retrieving what the caller may not see: a group field on each document plus a filter derived from the authenticated caller's identity makes the restriction a query-time predicate the model cannot talk its way around. Enforcement happens before any restricted text reaches the prompt.

An instruction is a request, not an access control — the restricted text is already in the model's context, so a prompt injection, an ambiguous question, or plain model error can leak it. Access decisions must not be delegated to model compliance.

Filtering the output after generation means the restricted content was retrieved, sent to the model, and influenced the answer even if a citation is stripped. Summaries and paraphrases carry the leaked information without the citation the filter looks for.

Content filters classify harmful content categories such as hate or violence; they have no notion of who the caller is or which practice group owns a document. This misapplies a safety control to an authorization problem.
principle: enforce entitlements at retrieval time, never in the prompt or the output
relatedConcept: Knowledge integration choices for agents differ in what they can enforce: an Azure AI Search connection supports filters over document metadata, which is what per-user trimming requires.
overallExplanation: Per-user entitlements are enforced by filtering the retrieval query on document metadata, so restricted content never enters the context. Instructions, output scrubbing, and content filters all operate after the leak has already happened.

question: A finance operations agent in Foundry Agent Service must do two things: compute variance statistics and produce a chart from CSV exports that analysts upload during the conversation, and file an approved journal entry in the ERP system by triggering an existing enterprise workflow that already runs in Azure Logic Apps. Which two tool integrations should you configure? (Choose two.)
options: The code interpreter tool, so the agent can run generated code against the uploaded CSV to compute statistics and render the chart
An Azure Logic Apps tool binding, so the agent can invoke the existing workflow that performs the ERP journal entry
A prompt instruction telling the agent to calculate the variance arithmetic itself and describe the chart in text
A custom function tool that reimplements the ERP posting logic in Python inside the agent's own service
optionExplanations: Correct. Code interpreter gives the agent a sandboxed execution environment for uploaded files, so numeric work is actually computed rather than predicted token by token, and chart images are produced as real output files. Deterministic arithmetic on user-supplied data is exactly the boundary where code beats generation.

Correct. Binding an existing Logic Apps workflow as a tool lets the agent invoke a process that already encodes the ERP connectivity, retries, and approvals, rather than duplicating it. Reusing the workflow also keeps the existing operational monitoring around that integration intact.

Asking a language model to do the arithmetic itself is precisely the failure mode code interpreter exists to prevent: results look plausible and are silently wrong, which is unacceptable in finance. A textual description of a chart is also not the chart the analysts asked for.

Reimplementing ERP posting inside the agent forks business-critical logic, duplicates credentials and error handling, and guarantees the two implementations drift. The existing Logic Apps workflow is already the tested path to the same system.
principle: compute with code, integrate through existing workflows
relatedConcept: Agent tool integration in Foundry spans code interpreter, function calling, OpenAPI tools, and connectors to Azure Functions and Logic Apps, so most enterprise actions are a binding rather than new code.

question: A German insurer must keep all inference processing for its claims assistant inside the European Union, confirmed in writing to its regulator. Which deployment option should they choose for the model?
options: A Data Zone Standard deployment in an EU-based Foundry resource, so traffic is processed within the EU data zone while still billing per token
A Global Standard deployment, because it offers the highest available throughput and the lowest per-token price
A Global Provisioned deployment, because provisioned capacity is dedicated to the customer and therefore stays in region
A Standard deployment in a single EU region with a manual failover script that redirects to a US region during the morning peak
optionExplanations: Correct. Data Zone Standard constrains processing to the data zone associated with the resource — for an EU resource, EU geographies — while keeping the pay-per-token consumption model the team wants until demand is predictable. It gives residency and burst headroom without a capacity commitment.

Global Standard routes requests to available capacity anywhere in the global fleet, which is exactly what the regulator's commitment forbids. Price and throughput are real advantages, but they do not survive a hard data-residency constraint.

Provisioned throughput reserves capacity, but the Global variant still routes globally — dedicated capacity is a performance and quota property, not a geographic one. It also forces the reserved commitment the team explicitly wanted to avoid.

Failing over to a US region during peak deliberately moves EU processing to the United States precisely when volume is highest. Regional Standard is a legitimate residency choice, but the failover design destroys the guarantee it provides.
principle: data residency is a deployment-type decision, not a resource-location one
relatedConcept: Foundry model deployment types trade off routing scope and cost: Global, Data Zone, and Regional variants exist for Standard, Provisioned, and Batch.

question: A trading-desk copilot runs a steady 1.4 million tokens per minute during market hours with a contractual p99 latency ceiling, and it currently sits on a Standard deployment where latency varies noticeably under load. Twice a week an unpredictable news event pushes demand roughly 40% above the steady baseline for a few minutes. What deployment configuration best meets both the latency ceiling and the spikes?
options: Provision a Provisioned Throughput deployment sized to the steady baseline and enable spillover to a Standard deployment so overflow traffic is served during spikes
Provision a Provisioned Throughput deployment sized for the twice-weekly peak so the reserved capacity never runs out
Keep the Standard deployment and add aggressive client-side retries with exponential backoff to absorb the spikes
Create three Standard deployments of the same model and round-robin requests across them to smooth the latency distribution
optionExplanations: Correct. Provisioned throughput gives the dedicated, predictable latency the contractual p99 requires for the steady load, and spillover routes the overflow that exceeds provisioned capacity to a Standard deployment instead of returning errors. Sizing to baseline rather than peak is what keeps the reservation economical.

Sizing reserved capacity to a peak that occurs for a few minutes twice a week means paying full time for capacity that idles almost always. Provisioned throughput is a commitment, so overprovisioning is a pure cost decision with no latency benefit at baseline.

Retries with backoff make a client survive throttling; they do nothing for the p99 latency ceiling and in fact add latency to the very requests that were slow. Standard deployments share capacity, which is the source of the variance being complained about.

Multiple Standard deployments draw on the same regional quota pool for the subscription, so this does not multiply available capacity and shared-capacity variance persists. It adds routing complexity while leaving the latency guarantee unmet.
principle: reserve capacity for the baseline and let spillover absorb the tail
relatedConcept: Choosing between Standard and Provisioned deployments is a latency-predictability decision; spillover exists so a provisioned deployment does not have to be sized for its worst minute.
overallExplanation: Provisioned throughput sized to steady load plus spillover to Standard meets a latency SLA without paying for peak capacity full time. Retries and extra Standard deployments do not change shared-capacity latency behaviour.

question: A retailer needs to generate product description summaries for 2.4 million catalogue items. The job runs once, results are consumed by a nightly publishing pipeline, and anything finishing within 24 hours is fine. The team's first attempt looped the items through their interactive Standard deployment and immediately began throttling the customer-facing chat app that shares the same quota. What is the right deployment choice for this job?
options: Submit the work to a Global Batch deployment, which processes the job asynchronously against separate batch quota at a reduced token price
Keep the Standard deployment but add a fixed sleep between requests so the loop stays under the throttling threshold
Request a large temporary quota increase for the Standard deployment and run the loop with more parallelism
Create a Provisioned Throughput deployment for the duration of the job and delete it when the catalogue is finished
optionExplanations: Correct. Batch deployments exist for exactly this shape of work: a large offline job with a 24-hour completion target, priced well below Standard and drawing on its own enqueued token quota so it does not compete with interactive traffic. Submitting a file of requests also removes the hand-written throttling loop entirely.

Sleeping between requests keeps the loop under the limit but stretches 2.4 million items across an impractical wall-clock window and still consumes the shared interactive quota the whole time. It manages the symptom rather than moving the work off the interactive path.

Raising Standard quota to accommodate a one-off bulk job means the interactive app and the batch loop still share one pool, so a burst in either can starve the other. It also pays full interactive token prices for work with no latency requirement.

Provisioned throughput is a reserved-capacity commitment tuned for predictable low latency, which this job does not need, and it is billed accordingly. Standing one up for a single overnight run is the most expensive way to solve a latency-insensitive problem.
principle: latency-insensitive bulk work belongs on batch quota, not interactive quota
relatedConcept: Deployment options in Foundry include Standard, Provisioned, and Batch; picking correctly starts with the workload's latency requirement, not its size.
overallExplanation: A one-off 2.4 million item job with a 24-hour window is the canonical Global Batch case: separate quota, asynchronous processing, and a lower token price. Throttling loops and quota increases keep bulk work on the interactive path where it damages the user-facing app.

domain: Plan and manage an Azure AI solution
objective: Set up AI solutions in Foundry
question: Your Foundry project lives in a resource in North Europe. A newly released multimodal model appears in the model catalog, but when you try to create a Standard deployment in that resource the model is not offered, and the model's documentation lists a smaller set of supported regions that excludes North Europe. The application must call this model within two weeks. What is the correct action?
options: Create the model deployment in a Foundry resource located in one of the model's supported regions and have the application call that deployment's endpoint, adding a project connection to it
Open a support request to have the model enabled in North Europe, since regional model availability is a per-subscription allowlist
Deploy the closest previous-generation model available in North Europe and rely on prompt engineering to reproduce the newer model's multimodal behaviour
Recreate the entire Foundry project and all of its connections in a supported region, since a project cannot reference a deployment outside its own region
optionExplanations: Correct. Model availability is per region and per deployment type, so the working pattern is to place the deployment where the model is actually offered and reference it from the application, wiring it up as a connection so credentials and endpoints stay managed. Nothing forces model deployments to sit in the same region as every other component.

Regional availability reflects where Microsoft has enabled the model's capacity, not a per-subscription entitlement flag, so a support ticket cannot conjure a region into the supported list. This wastes the two-week window waiting on a request that will not be granted.
Substituting an older model abandons the multimodal capability the requirement is built on, and prompting cannot add a modality a model does not support. This is a downgrade dressed as a workaround.

Rebuilding the project is a large, disruptive migration justified by a constraint that does not exist — applications routinely call deployments in other regions. If the whole solution needs to move for latency reasons that is a separate decision, not a prerequisite for using this model.
principle: check regional model availability before choosing where things live
relatedConcept: Designing Azure infrastructure for AI apps includes placing model deployments where the chosen models and deployment types are actually offered, and connecting projects to them.
overallExplanation: When a model is not available in your project's region, deploy it in a supported region and reference that deployment through a connection. Regional availability is a capacity fact, not a subscription toggle, and it does not require rebuilding the project.

domain: Plan and manage an Azure AI solution
objective: Set up AI solutions in Foundry
question: A regulated healthcare summarizer passed validation against a specific model version and the evidence pack cites that version. Six weeks later the clinical review board reports that outputs changed format overnight; the deployment's version upgrade policy is set to auto-update to default, and the model's default version had rolled forward. What should the team configure going forward?
options: Pin the deployment to a specific model version and introduce a controlled process that validates each new version on a separate deployment before switching production over
Leave auto-update enabled but add a nightly regression test that alerts the team when the output format changes
Set the deployment to auto-update but lower temperature to zero so the newer version produces the same output as the validated one
Create a second deployment of the same model version and load balance across both so an upgrade only affects half the traffic
optionExplanations: Correct. Pinning the version makes the production deployment immutable with respect to Microsoft's default-version rollouts, which is what a validated, evidence-backed clinical workflow requires. Validating the next version on a parallel deployment first turns the upgrade into a deliberate, testable release rather than an overnight surprise.

A nightly regression test detects the change after users have already received differently formatted summaries, and in a regulated workflow that is a documented incident. Detection is valuable, but it does not substitute for preventing an unreviewed model change in production.

Temperature controls sampling randomness within one model version; it cannot make a newer version reproduce an older one's formatting or behaviour. This confuses run-to-run variance with version-to-version change.

Load balancing across two deployments of the same version does nothing once the default version rolls forward, because the same auto-update policy applies to both. It halves nothing and adds a second thing to manage.
principle: validated workloads pin the model version and upgrade on purpose
relatedConcept: Configuring model deployments includes the version upgrade policy, which decides whether Microsoft's default-version rollouts reach production automatically.
overallExplanation: Pin the model version for validated workloads and qualify each new version on a separate deployment before promoting it. Auto-update plus monitoring detects the change only after users are affected, and sampling settings cannot mask a version difference.

question: A Python service that calls a Foundry project is being promoted from dev to test to prod. Today the project endpoint URL, the model deployment name, and an API key are all literals in the source, and each environment has its own Foundry resource. Which two changes should the CI/CD pipeline introduce so the same build artefact runs correctly in every environment? (Choose two.)
options: Read the project endpoint and the model deployment name from environment configuration injected per environment by the pipeline
Authenticate with DefaultAzureCredential so the same code uses a developer identity locally and the workload's managed identity in each deployed environment
Keep the values in source but add an if statement that selects the right endpoint based on the hostname the service is running on
Publish separate branches of the repository per environment so each branch carries the correct literal endpoint and key
optionExplanations: Correct. Endpoints and deployment names are environment facts, not code, so injecting them as configuration is what lets one immutable artefact be promoted through the pipeline unchanged. It also means a new environment is a config change rather than a code change and rebuild.

Correct. DefaultAzureCredential resolves whatever identity is available — a signed-in developer locally, the assigned managed identity in Azure — so the credential acquisition path stops being environment-specific code. As a bonus it removes the API key literal that should never have been in source at all.

Hostname sniffing hardcodes the environment topology into the application, so every new environment or renamed host requires a code change and a redeploy. It also leaves the secrets in source control, which is the more serious of the two problems here.

Per-environment branches guarantee configuration drift: fixes land on one branch and not others, and the thing tested in test is literally not the thing shipped to prod. Branching is for code changes, not for deployment configuration.
principle: build once, configure per environment, and never ship credentials in source
relatedConcept: Integrating Foundry projects with CI/CD means parameterizing endpoints, deployment names, and resource ids, and letting managed identity supply credentials at run time.
overallExplanation: Promote one artefact by injecting endpoint and deployment name as per-environment configuration and by acquiring credentials through DefaultAzureCredential. Hostname branching and per-environment repository branches both hardcode topology and invite drift.

question: A bank is moving an internal agent from a proof of concept to production. Audit requires that conversation threads, uploaded files, and the vector store used for agent knowledge all live in subscriptions the bank owns, inside its own storage accounts, with customer-managed keys where applicable. Which setup should the team use for Foundry Agent Service?
options: Use the standard agent setup, bringing your own Azure Cosmos DB account, Azure Storage account, and Azure AI Search service and connecting them to the project
Use the basic agent setup and add a nightly export job that copies threads and files into the bank's own storage account
Use the basic agent setup and enable customer-managed keys on the Foundry resource, which relocates thread and file storage into the bank's subscription
Skip Agent Service and rebuild the agent loop directly against the model deployment, storing everything in the bank's own database
optionExplanations: Correct. The standard agent setup exists to let customers bring their own Cosmos DB for thread storage, Storage account for files, and AI Search for the vector store, so agent state resides in resources the bank owns and governs. That is the configuration that satisfies an audit demand for customer-owned data stores rather than platform-managed ones.

A nightly export makes a copy; the authoritative data still lives in platform-managed storage for up to a day, which is precisely what the audit finding is about. It also adds a synchronization job that can silently fall behind.

Customer-managed keys change who controls the encryption key, not where the data physically resides. Conflating key ownership with data residency is a common exam trap and would not close the audit item.

Hand-rolling the agent loop discards managed tools, thread management, and tracing, and replaces a supported configuration option with a large amount of code to maintain. The platform already offers a bring-your-own-resources mode for this exact requirement.
principle: bring-your-own-resources is a setup choice, not something you bolt on later
relatedConcept: Designing Azure infrastructure for agent solutions includes choosing between basic and standard agent setup, which determines whether thread, file, and vector storage is platform-managed or customer-owned.
overallExplanation: Standard agent setup with your own Cosmos DB, Storage, and AI Search puts agent state in customer-owned resources, which is what data-governance audits require. Exports copy data after the fact and customer-managed keys control encryption, not location.

question: Security requires that a Foundry resource be reachable only from the company's virtual network. You created a private endpoint for the resource in the app subnet and disabled public network access. From a VM in that VNet, calls now fail during connection setup, and nslookup for the resource host returns a public IP address in the 20.x range. What is missing?
options: The private DNS zone for the service is not linked to the virtual network, so the host name is still resolving to the public endpoint instead of the private IP
The application is missing a role assignment on the Foundry resource, which is why the connection is refused after public access was disabled
The private endpoint needs public network access left enabled until the DNS records propagate, so disabling it too early breaks resolution
The subnet is missing a service endpoint for Azure AI services, which is what rewrites the host name to the private address
optionExplanations: Correct. A private endpoint gives the resource a private IP, but clients only use it if name resolution returns that IP — which requires the matching privatelink DNS zone to contain the A record and to be linked to the VNet. A public IP in the nslookup result is the definitive signature of the missing zone link.

An authorization problem surfaces as an HTTP 403 after a connection and a successful token exchange, not as a failure during connection setup with a public IP in DNS. This misreads a network-layer symptom as an RBAC one.

Private DNS records are created with the private endpoint and do not need public access as a fallback while they settle; leaving public access on would merely mask the resolution bug. The design goal was to close the public path in the first place.

Service endpoints and private endpoints are different mechanisms: service endpoints keep traffic on the Azure backbone from the subnet but do not create a private IP or change DNS resolution. Only the private DNS zone makes the host name resolve privately.
principle: a private endpoint without private DNS resolves to the public address
relatedConcept: Designing Azure infrastructure for AI apps includes the network path: private endpoint, private DNS zone linked to the VNet, and public network access disabled on the resource.
overallExplanation: Private endpoints require the corresponding privatelink private DNS zone to be linked to the VNet, or clients keep resolving the public IP. Public-IP resolution is a DNS symptom, not an RBAC or service-endpoint one.

question: A GitHub Actions workflow deploys Foundry infrastructure and model deployments using a service principal client secret stored as a repository secret. The secret expired at 2 a.m., breaking the release, and the security team has flagged long-lived credentials in CI as a finding. What should the team change in the pipeline's authentication?
options: Configure workload identity federation so the workflow exchanges its GitHub OIDC token for an Azure AD token, removing the stored client secret entirely
Move the client secret into Azure Key Vault and have the workflow fetch it at the start of each run
Extend the service principal secret expiry to the maximum allowed and add a calendar reminder before it lapses
Switch the workflow to use the Foundry resource's API key, since keys do not expire on a fixed schedule
optionExplanations: Correct. Federated credentials let the workflow present its short-lived GitHub OIDC token and receive an Azure AD access token in exchange, so there is no secret to store, rotate, or expire. It also scopes trust to a specific repository, branch, or environment, which is stronger than any secret sitting in a settings page.

Key Vault protects the secret at rest, but the workflow still needs a credential to authenticate to Key Vault, so a long-lived secret exists somewhere and the expiry problem is merely relocated. It reduces exposure without removing the class of failure.

A longer expiry postpones the outage and leaves a highly privileged, long-lived credential in CI — the exact security finding raised. Calendar reminders are a process control standing in for a technical one.

Resource API keys are static shared secrets with broad data-plane access and no per-pipeline identity, so this is a step backwards from a service principal. Keys also cannot perform the control-plane operations needed to create deployments.
principle: prefer federated, short-lived identity over any stored secret in CI
relatedConcept: Integrating Foundry projects with CI/CD includes how the pipeline authenticates to Azure, which sets the blast radius of the automation identity.
overallExplanation: Workload identity federation replaces stored client secrets with a short-lived OIDC token exchange scoped to the repository, eliminating both the expiry outage and the long-lived credential finding. Vaulting or extending the secret only moves or delays the problem.

domain: Plan and manage an Azure AI solution
objective: Set up AI solutions in Foundry
question: A platform team runs dev, test, and prod for an AI product inside one Foundry resource, separating environments only by naming conventions such as chat-dev and chat-prod on deployments and connections. A load test against chat-dev exhausted the shared regional token quota and prod requests began failing. Auditors have separately asked how prod access is restricted. How should the environments be restructured?
options: Give each environment its own Foundry resource and project in its own resource group, so quota, role assignments, and connections are isolated per environment
Keep the single resource but rename the deployments with a stricter prefix scheme and document which prefixes are production
Keep the single resource and apply Azure Policy to deny changes to any deployment whose name ends with -prod
Keep the single resource and move dev traffic to a second region while leaving prod where it is
optionExplanations: Correct. Quota is tracked per subscription and region for a model, and role assignments and connections are scoped to the resource, so separating environments into their own resources is what actually isolates both the throughput blast radius and the access boundary. It also gives auditors a clean scope to point at for who can reach production.

Naming conventions are documentation, not enforcement: a prefix cannot stop a load test from consuming shared quota or stop a developer's role assignment from covering prod. It addresses neither the outage nor the audit question.

Azure Policy on names can block certain control-plane operations, but the incident was data-plane token consumption, which policy does not throttle. It also leaves data-plane permissions identical across environments.

Splitting regions can relieve the quota collision, but the two environments still share a resource, its role assignments, its connections, and its content filter configuration. It fixes one symptom and leaves the access-isolation finding untouched.
principle: environment isolation means separate resources, not separate names
relatedConcept: Designing Azure infrastructure for AI solutions includes the resource topology, because quota, RBAC scope, and connections are all resource- and subscription-scoped facts.
overallExplanation: Separate Foundry resources per environment isolate quota consumption and give distinct RBAC and connection scopes. Naming conventions and policies on names provide no runtime isolation for either throughput or access.

question: A team promotes changes to a customer-facing Foundry application every sprint, and the last two releases regressed answer groundedness without anyone noticing until support tickets arrived. They want the release pipeline itself to catch this class of regression before all users are exposed. Which two pipeline practices should they add? (Choose two.)
options: Run an automated evaluation of the release candidate against a versioned golden dataset in the pipeline, failing the stage when scores such as groundedness fall below an agreed threshold
Roll the release out to a small percentage of traffic first and compare production quality and safety signals against the current version before completing the rollout
Increase unit test coverage of the application's Python code until every prompt-building function is exercised by a test
Require two human reviewers to approve the prompt diff in the pull request before the release is allowed to proceed
optionExplanations: Correct. A golden dataset plus quality evaluators turns groundedness into a measurable gate a build can fail, which is the only way a pipeline catches a regression automatically. Versioning the dataset means the threshold comparison is like-for-like across releases rather than drifting with the test data.

Correct. Offline evaluation cannot cover every real query distribution, so a staged or canary rollout with production quality and safety signals compared against the incumbent limits exposure while giving real-world evidence. It is the natural complement to a pre-deployment gate.

Unit tests verify that prompt-building code does what the developer intended; they say nothing about whether the resulting answers are grounded in the retrieved sources. Perfect coverage of deterministic code is compatible with a serious quality regression.

Human review of a prompt diff is useful hygiene but is a subjective judgement made without measurement, and reviewers are exactly who missed the last two regressions. It adds latency to releases without producing a score anyone can compare.
principle: gate releases on measured quality, then expose gradually
relatedConcept: Integrating Foundry projects with CI/CD includes automated evaluation stages and staged rollout, because generative regressions are invisible to conventional software tests.
overallExplanation: Catch generative regressions with an automated evaluation gate against a versioned golden dataset, then limit exposure with a canary rollout compared to the incumbent. Code coverage and human prompt review do not measure answer quality.

question: Two workloads share one model in the same region: an interactive assistant that must stay responsive, and a nightly enrichment job. Both currently call the same Standard deployment, and the enrichment job regularly consumes most of the tokens per minute, throttling the assistant. The subscription's total regional quota for that model cannot be increased right now. What deployment configuration resolves the contention?
options: Create two deployments of the model and allocate a fixed share of the available tokens-per-minute capacity to each, sizing the interactive deployment for its peak and giving the remainder to the enrichment job
Keep one deployment and have the enrichment job retry with a longer backoff whenever it receives HTTP 429
Keep one deployment and raise its capacity setting to a value above the subscription's remaining regional quota so it can burst when needed
Move the enrichment job to a different model family that has separate documentation, so the two workloads no longer interact
optionExplanations: Correct. Deployment capacity is expressed in tokens per minute drawn from the region's quota for that model, so splitting the pool across two deployments creates a hard ceiling on what the enrichment job can consume. The interactive workload then has a reserved share that a runaway batch cannot take.

Longer backoff makes the batch job politer, but both workloads still draw from one shared limit and the assistant is still throttled whenever the job happens to be in flight. Client-side manners are not capacity isolation.

A deployment's capacity cannot exceed the unallocated quota available in the region, so the request simply fails rather than granting burst headroom. This misunderstands capacity as a soft hint rather than an allocation from a fixed pool.

Model family does not determine quota isolation by itself, and swapping models to dodge contention changes output characteristics the enrichment pipeline was validated against. It also leaves the same contention pattern in place if the new model shares regional capacity.
principle: isolate workloads by allocating capacity, not by asking them to behave
relatedConcept: Configuring model deployments includes assigning tokens-per-minute capacity from the region's quota, which is how competing workloads are given independent ceilings.
overallExplanation: Split the regional quota into two deployments with explicit tokens-per-minute allocations so batch work cannot starve interactive traffic. Backoff and oversized capacity requests do not create isolation within a single shared deployment.

domain: Plan and manage an Azure AI solution
objective: Manage, monitor, and secure AI systems
question: During a product launch, your Python service starts receiving HTTP 429 responses from a Standard model deployment on roughly 12% of calls. The responses carry a retry-after header, average token usage per request is unchanged, and the deployment is running at its assigned tokens-per-minute ceiling. The current client immediately retries three times in a tight loop. What is the correct short-term and long-term response?
options: Honour the retry-after value and retry with exponential backoff plus jitter, and in parallel request additional quota so the deployment's tokens-per-minute allocation matches launch demand
Rotate the resource key and recreate the client, since 429 indicates the current credential has exhausted its allowance
Catch the 429 and fall back to returning a cached generic answer to the user, so the error rate reported by the service drops to zero
Remove the retry logic entirely so failed calls surface immediately and users can resubmit their request themselves
optionExplanations: Correct. HTTP 429 is a rate-limit signal, and the service tells you how long to wait through retry-after; honouring it with exponential backoff and jitter stops the tight retry loop from amplifying the congestion it is reacting to. Backoff only smooths the peak, so the durable fix is raising the deployment's tokens-per-minute allocation to match sustained launch demand.

Keys authenticate; they do not carry per-credential throughput allowances, so rotating one changes nothing about the rate limit. This confuses a throttling response with an authentication failure, which would be a 401.

Serving a cached generic answer hides a capacity problem behind a degraded user experience and makes the metric that would have triggered a quota increase look healthy. Suppressing the signal is how a launch-day capacity issue becomes a silent quality issue.

Removing retries makes every transient throttle a user-visible failure, when a brief backoff would have succeeded. Transient rate limiting is precisely the case retry logic exists for — the bug is the tight loop, not the retry.
principle: 429 means slow down and get more capacity, not re-authenticate
relatedConcept: Managing rate limits means combining client-side behaviour — respecting retry-after, exponential backoff, jitter — with capacity planning through quota allocation.
overallExplanation: Answer a 429 by honouring retry-after with exponential backoff and jitter, then raise the deployment's tokens-per-minute quota for sustained demand. Key rotation targets authentication, and cached fallbacks merely hide the capacity shortfall.

domain: Plan and manage an Azure AI solution
