question: Finance reports that the AI platform's monthly bill grew from $22,000 to $61,000 across a quarter. Four internal applications share one Foundry resource, and nobody can say which application drove the increase because every app authenticates with the same resource key and calls the same deployment. What should the platform team do first?
options: Give each application its own deployment and identity, then use Azure Monitor metrics for token usage split by deployment to attribute spend before deciding what to optimize
Halve the max_tokens setting on the shared deployment so every application's responses get cheaper immediately
Move all four applications to a smaller model, since the increase is clearly driven by model choice
Set a budget alert on the subscription so finance is notified when spend passes $50,000 next month
optionExplanations: Correct. You cannot optimize what you cannot attribute, and per-application deployments with distinct identities make processed-token metrics in Azure Monitor break down by consumer. Once one application is identified as the growth driver, the optimization — caching, a smaller model, prompt trimming — can be targeted instead of guessed.

Cutting max_tokens across all four applications truncates legitimate long answers for every consumer to address a cost driver that has not been identified. It is an untargeted quality regression justified by an assumption.

Model choice may be part of the story, but nothing in the evidence supports it, and forcing four different workloads onto a smaller model risks quality failures in the ones that needed the larger model. Diagnose the growth before changing every application's model.

A budget alert tells you the bill grew again next month, which is already known; it produces no attribution and no reduction. Alerting is a useful backstop but is not a first step towards cost control.
principle: attribute spend per consumer before optimizing anything
relatedConcept: Managing cost footprints starts with observability: per-deployment token metrics and per-application identities are what turn a single aggregate invoice into an actionable breakdown.
overallExplanation: Separate deployments and identities per application so Azure Monitor token metrics attribute spend, then optimize the actual driver. Blanket parameter cuts and model downgrades trade quality for savings without evidence.

domain: Plan and manage an Azure AI solution
objective: Manage, monitor, and secure AI systems
question: A summarization service ran unchanged for three months. Support now reports that summaries have become noticeably longer and less faithful to the source, but no application deployment happened. The deployment's version upgrade policy allows automatic updates and there is no continuous evaluation on production traffic. How should the team establish what happened and prevent a repeat?
options: Compare the deployment's current model version against the version recorded when the service was validated, then add continuous evaluation that scores sampled production responses for groundedness and flags a drop
Restart the service and clear its response cache, since stale cached completions are the most likely cause of the change in output style
Ask users to rate individual summaries with a thumbs-up control and treat the resulting score as the drift detector
Retrain the embedding model used for retrieval, because embedding drift is the usual cause of longer outputs
optionExplanations: Correct. With no application change, the environment changed, and the auto-update policy makes the model version the prime suspect — comparing the current version to the validated one settles it in minutes. Adding continuous evaluation on sampled production traffic converts the next such change from a support ticket into an alert with a measured groundedness delta.

A cache would replay old outputs, which would make responses look unchanged rather than newly verbose. This inverts the symptom: cached content cannot explain a shift towards longer, less faithful summaries.

Thumbs-up feedback is sparse, biased towards the annoyed, and arrives without a reference answer, so it detects large failures late and small quality drifts never. It complements measured evaluation but cannot serve as the detector.

Embeddings do not change on their own, and nothing suggests retrieval quality moved; embedding models also do not control output length. This proposes an expensive re-index against a hypothesis with no supporting signal.
principle: when the code did not change, look at what the platform changed
relatedConcept: Monitoring model performance and drift covers change in the environment as well as change in the data — model version rollovers are a routine cause of unexplained behaviour shifts.
overallExplanation: Unexplained quality shifts with no code deployment point at a model version rollover under an auto-update policy. Continuous evaluation of sampled production traffic for groundedness is what detects the next one automatically.

domain: Plan and manage an Azure AI solution
objective: Manage, monitor, and secure AI systems
question: A RAG assistant over 90,000 support articles is in production. Leadership wants an ongoing measure of whether answers stay anchored to retrieved sources, with alerting when the measure degrades, but the team cannot afford to have humans label every production answer. Which monitoring design fits the requirement?
options: Enable continuous evaluation on a sampled percentage of production traces, scoring each sampled response with groundedness and relevance evaluators, and alert on a sustained score drop
Log every prompt and response to a storage account and have a reviewer read a random 20 answers each morning
Track average response latency and token counts as proxies, since a poorly grounded answer generally takes longer to produce
Rerun the pre-release offline evaluation suite weekly and treat its scores as the production quality measure
optionExplanations: Correct. Continuous evaluation scores a sample of real production traces with model-graded evaluators such as groundedness and relevance, which gives an ongoing, unlabelled quality signal that can drive alerts. Sampling controls the evaluation cost while still tracking the trend leadership asked for.

Twenty manual reads a day covers a vanishing fraction of traffic, produces no consistent numeric series, and cannot support alerting. It is useful qualitative review on top of measurement, not a substitute for it.

Latency and token counts are operational metrics with no reliable relationship to groundedness — a confidently fabricated short answer is fast and cheap. Proxy metrics here would give false assurance precisely when quality fails.

The offline suite uses a fixed golden dataset, so rerunning it weekly against unchanged questions mostly re-measures the same thing and misses shifts in what real users ask. It validates releases; it does not monitor production.
principle: monitor grounding quality on sampled production traffic, not on the release test set
relatedConcept: Monitoring grounding quality uses the same evaluators as pre-release testing, but applied continuously to sampled live traces so drift shows up as a trend.
overallExplanation: Continuous evaluation over sampled production traces with groundedness and relevance evaluators gives an affordable, alertable quality signal. Manual spot reads, operational proxies, and reruns of the offline suite all miss live drift.

domain: Plan and manage an Azure AI solution
objective: Manage, monitor, and secure AI systems
question: After a content migration, users of a knowledge assistant complain that recently published articles are never cited and some answers reference material that was deleted weeks ago. The Azure AI Search index is refreshed by a scheduled indexer with a skillset. Which two monitoring signals should the team put in place to catch this class of problem going forward? (Choose two.)
options: Alert on indexer execution history showing failed or skipped documents and on the gap between source document count and indexed document count
Track retrieval quality over a fixed set of golden queries with known correct documents, alerting when ranking metrics regress after an index refresh
Alert whenever the search service's query volume per minute changes by more than 10% week over week
Alert whenever the average length of indexed documents changes, since content changes usually show up as length changes first
optionExplanations: Correct. Silent indexer failures and document-count divergence are the direct explanation for both symptoms — new articles never arrived and deleted ones were never removed — and both are visible in indexer execution history and count comparisons. This is the ingestion-health half of the problem.

Correct. A golden query set with known relevant documents converts relevance into a number that can be compared before and after each refresh, so a degradation in what gets retrieved is caught even when the pipeline reports success. This is the relevance half of the problem.

Query volume measures user demand, not index correctness — an index can be badly stale while traffic is perfectly flat. It would alert on marketing campaigns and holidays rather than on ingestion faults.

Average document length is a weak and noisy proxy that moves for entirely benign editorial reasons and would not budge when a handful of new articles fail to index. It monitors a statistic nobody has tied to the failure mode.
principle: watch both that content arrived and that the right content ranks
relatedConcept: Monitoring data ingestion quality, index health, and relevance performance are three distinct checks; pipeline success alone does not prove retrieval still works.
overallExplanation: Monitor indexer execution history and document-count parity for ingestion health, and a golden query set with ranking metrics for relevance. Traffic volume and document-length statistics are unrelated to whether the index is complete or ranking correctly.

domain: Plan and manage an Azure AI solution
objective: Manage, monitor, and secure AI systems
question: A Python API running in Azure Container Apps uses DefaultAzureCredential with a user-assigned managed identity to call a Foundry model deployment. Logs show the token request succeeds and returns an access token for the cognitive services scope, but the very next call fails with HTTP 403 and a message about the principal lacking permission over the resource. What is the fix?
options: Assign the managed identity an appropriate data-plane role such as Cognitive Services OpenAI User on the Foundry resource scope
Recreate the user-assigned managed identity and re-attach it to the container app, because its credentials have gone stale
Switch the client from token authentication to the resource API key, which does not depend on role assignments
Add the container app's outbound IP addresses to the resource's network allow list so the calls are accepted
optionExplanations: Correct. A successful token acquisition proves authentication worked — Entra ID knows who the principal is — so a subsequent 403 is an authorization verdict, which is settled by a role assignment at the correct scope. Data-plane calls to a model deployment need a data-plane role such as Cognitive Services OpenAI User, which control-plane roles like Contributor do not imply.

Managed identity credentials are issued and rotated by the platform, and the evidence shows a token was issued successfully, so nothing is stale. Recreating the identity also invalidates any role assignments that do exist, making the situation worse.

Falling back to a key trades a diagnosable authorization gap for a long-lived shared secret and abandons the keyless posture the design chose. It makes the error disappear without anyone understanding which permissions the workload actually needs.

A network restriction produces a connection-level rejection or a 403 citing a network rule, and it would prevent the call from being evaluated against a principal at all. The message names the principal's permissions, which points squarely at RBAC.
principle: a 403 after a successful token means RBAC, not authentication
relatedConcept: Securing AI systems with managed identity separates authentication (getting a token) from authorization (having a data-plane role at the right scope) — the error code tells you which one failed.
overallExplanation: Token acquired plus 403 equals missing role assignment; grant the managed identity a data-plane role such as Cognitive Services OpenAI User at the resource scope. Recreating identities or falling back to keys mistakes an authorization gap for an authentication one.

domain: Plan and manage an Azure AI solution
objective: Manage, monitor, and secure AI systems
question: A security review finds that a Foundry resource's API keys are pasted into three application settings, a notebook, and one archived support ticket. The team migrates every workload to DefaultAzureCredential with managed identity and grants the required roles, and all applications verify successfully. What remaining step best guarantees the leaked keys can no longer be used?
options: Disable local authentication on the resource so key-based access is rejected outright and only Entra ID tokens are accepted
Regenerate both keys on the resource so the copies that leaked stop working
Store the keys in Azure Key Vault and restrict access to the vault with RBAC
Add a diagnostic setting that logs key-based requests so the team can investigate anyone still using them
optionExplanations: Correct. Disabling local authentication removes key-based access as a mechanism, so the resource only honours Entra ID tokens and no leaked or future key can be replayed. Once every workload is already on managed identity, this is the step that makes the keyless posture enforced rather than merely adopted.

Regenerating invalidates the specific leaked values, but the resource still accepts key authentication, so the next key that ends up in a notebook or a ticket is just as dangerous. It is remediation for one incident rather than removal of the attack surface.

Key Vault is the right answer when you must keep using a secret, but here the workloads no longer need keys at all. Vaulting an unnecessary credential preserves the mechanism you were trying to eliminate.
Logging key usage gives visibility after the fact and depends on someone acting on the alert. It is a detective control where a preventive one is available at no operational cost.
principle: keyless is only real once local authentication is disabled
relatedConcept: Configuring keyless credentials is a two-part change: move workloads to managed identity with role assignments, then switch off key-based authentication on the resource.
overallExplanation: Disabling local authentication is what stops leaked keys from ever working again, and it is safe once every workload uses managed identity. Regenerating keys, vaulting them, or logging their use all leave key-based access enabled.

domain: Plan and manage an Azure AI solution
objective: Manage, monitor, and secure AI systems
question: A public-sector customer requires that a Foundry resource and its connected Azure AI Search service be unreachable from the internet, with all traffic from their application subnet traversing the Microsoft backbone. The team has already deployed the applications into a virtual network. Which two configuration steps are required? (Choose two.)
options: Create private endpoints for the Foundry resource and the search service and link the corresponding privatelink private DNS zones to the virtual network
Set public network access to disabled on both resources so requests arriving over the public endpoint are refused
Assign a network security group rule that denies outbound internet traffic from the application subnet on port 443
Route all outbound traffic through an Azure Firewall with the resources' public host names allowed in an application rule
optionExplanations: Correct. Private endpoints give each resource a private IP inside the VNet, and linking the matching privatelink DNS zones is what makes clients resolve the host names to those private addresses instead of the public ones. Without both halves the traffic never leaves the public path.

Correct. A private endpoint adds a private path but does not by itself close the public one, so the resource remains reachable from the internet until public network access is disabled. Turning it off is what converts a private option into a private-only requirement.

Blocking outbound 443 from the subnet breaks every other HTTPS dependency the application has and still does nothing about inbound reachability of the AI resources from elsewhere on the internet. It is a blunt egress control aimed at the wrong direction.

Firewall application rules with allowed public host names keep traffic on the public endpoints, which is exactly what the requirement forbids, and add a hop without changing the path. Egress filtering complements private endpoints; it does not replace them.
principle: private endpoint plus private DNS, then close the public door
relatedConcept: Private networking for AI resources is a pair of changes — establish the private path with endpoints and DNS, then disable public network access so nothing falls back to it.
overallExplanation: Private endpoints with linked privatelink DNS zones create the private path, and disabling public network access removes the public one. Egress blocking and firewall allow-lists on public host names address neither requirement.

domain: Plan and manage an Azure AI solution
objective: Manage, monitor, and secure AI systems
question: Trust and safety asks to be alerted within an hour whenever content filter activity on a customer-facing assistant spikes, since a surge of blocked prompts has previously signalled a coordinated abuse campaign. Today nobody can see filter activity outside individual request responses. What should the platform team implement?
options: Add a diagnostic setting on the resource that sends the relevant request and safety logs to a Log Analytics workspace, then create an alert rule on the rate of filtered requests
Have the application write its own counter to a text file whenever it receives a filtered response, and have someone check the file each morning
Rely on the resource overview blade in the portal, since filtered requests appear there as part of the default metrics chart
Lower the content filter severity thresholds so more requests are blocked, making the spike easier to notice in overall traffic volume
optionExplanations: Correct. Diagnostic settings stream the resource's logs into Log Analytics where they can be queried and used as the basis for an alert rule, which is what turns per-request filter results into a monitorable rate with a one-hour response target. It also gives trust and safety a queryable history when they investigate a campaign.

A local text file counter is not durable across instances or restarts, is invisible to anyone else, and a morning check cannot meet a one-hour alerting requirement. It reinvents telemetry badly instead of using the platform's diagnostics pipeline.

The default metrics view shows operational counters such as calls and latency and is not a substitute for safety log analysis or alerting. Watching a portal chart also relies on someone happening to be looking at it.

Deliberately blocking more legitimate content to make abuse easier to spot degrades the product for every honest user and still provides no alert. Threshold tuning is a policy decision, not a monitoring mechanism.
principle: safety events need a telemetry pipeline and an alert rule, not eyeballs
relatedConcept: Monitoring safety events means exporting resource logs through diagnostic settings so filter activity becomes a queryable, alertable time series alongside performance metrics.
overallExplanation: Route resource logs to Log Analytics with a diagnostic setting and alert on the rate of filtered requests to meet a one-hour detection target. Local counters, portal charts, and tightening thresholds provide no alerting path.

domain: Plan and manage an Azure AI solution
objective: Implement responsible AI across generative AI and agentic systems
question: A clinical documentation assistant used by hospital staff is blocking legitimate requests: notes describing patient self-harm risk assessments are refused because the self-harm category triggers at low severity under the default content filter. The organization has an approved use case and a clinical governance process, and high-severity content must still be blocked. What is the appropriate configuration?
options: Create a custom content filter configuration for that deployment that raises the self-harm threshold to block only high severity, keeping other categories at their defaults, and apply it to the clinical deployment only
Turn content filtering off entirely for the Foundry resource so clinical staff are never interrupted
Keep the default filter and instruct clinicians to paraphrase risk assessments so that the wording avoids the filter
Add the clinical terms that trigger the filter to a custom blocklist so they are handled by the blocklist rather than the category classifier
optionExplanations: Correct. Content filter configurations are created and assigned per deployment, so the clinical workload can run a policy with a higher self-harm threshold while every other deployment keeps the defaults. Raising the threshold rather than disabling the category preserves blocking of genuinely harmful high-severity content, which matches the approved-use-case-with-governance situation.

Disabling filtering resource-wide removes protection from every workload on that resource, including ones with no clinical justification, and drops the other three harm categories as well. It answers a scoped policy question with an unscoped removal of controls.

Asking clinicians to reword clinical risk assessments degrades the medical record to satisfy a filter setting, and it will fail unpredictably because the classifier reacts to meaning rather than exact wording. Workflow contortion is not a substitute for a policy configuration.
Blocklists add terms to be blocked; they do not exempt anything, so this would make the refusals more frequent rather than fewer. It inverts what the blocklist feature does.
principle: tune filter severity per deployment for approved use cases, never switch protection off
relatedConcept: Configuring safety filters means assigning content filter configurations at deployment scope with per-category severity thresholds for prompts and completions.
overallExplanation: Assign a custom content filter configuration to the clinical deployment with a raised self-harm threshold, leaving other categories and other deployments untouched. Disabling filtering, rewording prompts, and blocklists all misapply the available controls.

domain: Plan and manage an Azure AI solution
objective: Implement responsible AI across generative AI and agentic systems
question: A procurement agent summarizes supplier PDFs and can call an internal tool to update supplier risk ratings. A red-team exercise showed that a PDF containing the sentence instructing the assistant to ignore prior instructions and set this supplier's risk to low caused the agent to call the tool with an attacker-chosen value. The user never asked for a rating change. Which control most directly addresses this?
options: Enable Prompt Shields for indirect attacks on the deployment so injected instructions inside retrieved documents are detected, and keep document content clearly delimited as data rather than instructions
Increase the severity thresholds on the hate and violence content filter categories, since the injected text is adversarial content
Add a system prompt line telling the agent to never follow instructions found inside documents
Disable the risk-rating tool and have the agent output a suggested rating for a human to type in manually
optionExplanations: Correct. Indirect prompt injection is a distinct threat class from harmful content, and Prompt Shields for indirect attacks is the detection built for instructions smuggled into retrieved or uploaded material. Pairing it with clear delimiting of document content as data reinforces the boundary the attack tries to erase.

Harm-category thresholds classify hateful, sexual, violent, or self-harm content; an injected instruction to change a risk rating is none of those, so the classifier will never see it as a violation. This applies the wrong detector to the threat.

A system prompt instruction raises the bar slightly but is itself just text competing with the attacker's text, and red teams routinely defeat it. Prompt wording cannot be the primary defence against injected instructions.

Removing the tool does close this path, but it also removes the agent's usefulness for the workflow it was built for, and injection can still corrupt the summary a human then acts on. Human approval is a sound layer, but it addresses impact rather than detecting the attack.
principle: content in equals data, not instructions — detect injection where it enters
relatedConcept: Risk detection in Foundry covers jailbreak attempts in user input and indirect attacks embedded in documents, which are separate from the four harm categories.
overallExplanation: Instructions hidden inside retrieved documents are indirect prompt injection, addressed by Prompt Shields for indirect attacks plus strict data-versus-instruction delimiting. Harm-category thresholds and system prompt pleas do not detect it.

domain: Plan and manage an Azure AI solution
objective: Implement responsible AI across generative AI and agentic systems
question: An IT support agent with six tools passes every functional smoke test, yet operations report that it often calls the ticket-creation tool when the user only wanted a status check, and sometimes stops before completing a multistep request. The team wants a repeatable measurement of these behaviours across a 300-conversation regression set. Which instrumentation should they add?
options: Run agent-focused evaluators over the recorded runs, scoring intent resolution, tool call accuracy, and task adherence so each behaviour becomes a tracked metric
Score the agent with a text similarity evaluator that compares its final message to a reference answer for each conversation
Measure the proportion of runs that complete without raising an exception and treat that as the agent quality metric
Add more detail to the tool descriptions and re-run the smoke tests to confirm the problems have gone
optionExplanations: Correct. The reported failures are about understanding the request, choosing and parameterizing tools, and finishing the task — which map onto intent resolution, tool call accuracy, and task adherence evaluators respectively. Running them over a fixed 300-conversation set turns anecdotes into per-behaviour scores that can be compared release over release.

Final-message similarity ignores the trajectory entirely, so an agent that created a spurious ticket on the way to a well-worded answer still scores highly. The failures here live in the tool calls, not in the final wording.

Exception-free completion measures whether the code ran, not whether the agent did the right thing — every reported failure in this scenario happened without an exception. It is an availability metric masquerading as a quality metric.

Improving tool descriptions is a plausible remedy, but without measurement nobody can tell whether it helped, and smoke tests already pass while the behaviour is wrong. Fixing before measuring is how these regressions returned unnoticed in the first place.
principle: evaluate the trajectory, not just the final message
relatedConcept: Responsible AI instrumentation for agents includes evaluators aimed at agent behaviour — intent resolution, tool call accuracy, task adherence — alongside quality and safety evaluators.
overallExplanation: Agent misbehaviour in tool selection and task completion is measured with intent resolution, tool call accuracy, and task adherence evaluators over a fixed conversation set. Final-answer similarity and exception rates miss trajectory failures entirely.

domain: Plan and manage an Azure AI solution
objective: Implement responsible AI across generative AI and agentic systems
question: A consumer-facing wellbeing assistant is two weeks from general availability. The team has quality metrics from a golden dataset but has done no adversarial testing, and the risk review asks for evidence about how the assistant behaves when users deliberately push it towards harmful or unsafe responses. Which two activities should the team run before launch? (Choose two.)
options: Run an automated AI red teaming pass that generates adversarial prompts across harm categories and attack strategies, and record the attack success rate per category
Run safety evaluations that score generated responses for harmful content categories and jailbreak susceptibility, using an adversarial simulator to produce the test conversations
Increase the size of the existing golden dataset so the quality evaluators cover more ordinary user questions
Have the engineering team manually try a handful of jailbreak prompts they have seen on social media and note whether the assistant refuses
optionExplanations: Correct. Automated red teaming systematically generates adversarial prompts across risk categories and attack strategies and reports an attack success rate, which is the reproducible evidence a risk review can act on. Doing it before general availability means findings can still change the launch decision.

Correct. Safety evaluations score responses for harm categories and jailbreak susceptibility, and an adversarial simulator produces the hostile conversations these evaluators need as input. Together they measure how the assistant behaves under pressure rather than how it performs on cooperative questions.
Expanding the golden dataset improves confidence on ordinary questions, which the team already has, and adds nothing about adversarial behaviour. It answers a question that was not asked.

Ad-hoc manual jailbreak attempts are unsystematic, unrepeatable, and biased towards whichever attacks the engineers happened to read about. They may find something, but they cannot produce coverage or a metric to compare against the next release.
principle: adversarial evidence must be generated systematically and scored
relatedConcept: Safety evaluations and AI red teaming are the pre-launch half of responsible AI instrumentation, complementing the quality evaluators used for ordinary traffic.
overallExplanation: Before general availability, run automated red teaming for attack success rates and safety evaluations driven by an adversarial simulator. Larger golden datasets and improvised manual jailbreak attempts produce no systematic adversarial evidence.

domain: Plan and manage an Azure AI solution
objective: Implement responsible AI across generative AI and agentic systems
question: An internal audit of a Foundry agent asks the team to reconstruct, for a specific customer complaint from six weeks ago, what the agent was asked, which tools it invoked with which arguments, and which retrieved documents informed the answer. Today the application logs only the final assistant message and an HTTP status. What should the team implement?
options: Enable tracing for the agent so each run emits spans covering the messages, tool invocations and their arguments, and retrieval steps, exporting them to Application Insights with a retention period that covers the audit window
Increase the application's log level to debug and log the full request and response bodies from the Python service to standard output
Store every user question and final answer in a database table with a timestamp so complaints can be matched by date
Rerun the same question against the agent today and record what happens as the reconstruction of the original interaction
optionExplanations: Correct. Tracing captures the whole run as structured spans — messages, tool calls with arguments, retrieval operations — so an auditor can follow the causal chain rather than infer it from an output. Exporting to Application Insights with retention that spans the audit window is what makes a six-week-old interaction still available to query.

Debug-level body logging captures the outer HTTP call, not the agent's internal steps, so tool invocations and retrieval remain invisible. It also sprays unstructured, potentially sensitive payloads into console output with no correlation between related steps.

A question-and-answer table records the endpoints of the interaction and none of the middle, which is precisely what the audit asks for. Timestamps let you find the row; they do not explain the behaviour.

Replaying the question today exercises the current agent configuration, model version, and index contents, so it cannot evidence what happened six weeks ago. Non-determinism alone makes this an unsound reconstruction.
principle: audits need the trace of how an answer happened, not just the answer
relatedConcept: Auditing through trace logging records the full run — prompts, tool calls, retrieval — as correlated telemetry that outlives the request itself.
overallExplanation: Enable agent tracing to Application Insights with retention covering the audit period so runs can be reconstructed step by step. Debug logs, answer tables, and replays capture the wrong data or the wrong point in time.

domain: Plan and manage an Azure AI solution
objective: Implement responsible AI across generative AI and agentic systems
question: A regulator will review outputs of a lending guidance assistant and expects, for any archived answer, evidence of which source passages supported it and which system produced it. The assistant currently returns clean prose with no attribution, and the team argues that citations clutter the interface. What should the team add to satisfy the requirement?
options: Return and persist provenance metadata with every answer — the retrieved source identifiers and passages used, plus the model and deployment version and the content filter results — surfacing citations in the interface where appropriate
Persist only the final answer text along with a hash of the prompt, so the record is compact and tamper evident
Record the retrieval index name and the date on which the answer was produced, which together identify the source material
Ask the model to include a sentence at the end of each answer stating which documents it used, based on its own recollection
optionExplanations: Correct. Provenance is a record of the specific inputs and system state behind an output: the passage identifiers actually retrieved, the model and deployment version that generated the text, and the safety verdicts applied. Persisting that alongside the answer is what lets a reviewer six months later verify support for a claim rather than take it on trust.

A hash proves the prompt was not altered but reveals nothing about which sources supported the answer or which model version produced it. Tamper evidence is not the same property as traceability to sources.

An index name and a date identify a corpus that has changed since, not the passages that were actually retrieved for that answer. Two answers from the same index on the same day can rest on entirely different documents.

A model-authored recollection of its sources is generated text and can be confidently wrong, which is exactly the failure mode a regulator is guarding against. Provenance must be captured from the retrieval step, not narrated by the model.
principle: capture provenance from the pipeline, never from the model's own account
relatedConcept: Provenance metadata — retrieved passages, model and deployment version, filter outcomes — is the auditing counterpart to trace logging and is what makes an archived answer defensible.
overallExplanation: Persist the actual retrieved passage identifiers, the model and deployment version, and the filter results with each answer. Hashes, index names, and model-narrated source lists all fail to tie a specific output to the evidence that produced it.

domain: Plan and manage an Azure AI solution
objective: Implement responsible AI across generative AI and agentic systems
question: A retail refunds agent may issue refunds automatically up to $200, but policy says anything above that must be approved by a human supervisor before money moves. In pre-production testing the agent issued a $2,400 refund after a persistent customer argued the case across several turns. The current control is a line in the system prompt stating the $200 limit. How should the control be implemented?
options: Enforce the threshold outside the model: have the refund tool require an explicit human approval step for amounts above $200 and reject unapproved calls server-side
Strengthen the system prompt with capitalized emphasis and repeat the $200 limit at the start and end of the instructions
Add a second model call that reviews the proposed refund and vetoes amounts above the threshold before the tool executes
Lower the agent's temperature to zero so it follows the stated policy deterministically
optionExplanations: Correct. A monetary limit is a business rule and must live where it cannot be argued with — in the tool implementation, which rejects any above-threshold call lacking a recorded approval. Making high-impact actions require an approval step is the standard safeguard for semiautonomous workflows, and it holds regardless of how persuasive the conversation was.

Emphasis and repetition change the odds, not the guarantee, and the incident already demonstrates that sustained user pressure overcomes prompt instructions. A policy that can be negotiated away is not a control.

A reviewing model call adds a probabilistic gate that is itself susceptible to the same persuasion, and it can be fed the same misleading framing. It is a reasonable extra signal but cannot be the enforcement point for a financial limit.

Temperature affects sampling randomness within the model's behaviour; it does not turn an instruction into an enforced constraint. A deterministic model can deterministically follow a persuasive argument to the wrong conclusion.
principle: high-impact actions are gated in code with approval, never by instructions
relatedConcept: Approval workflows are the human-in-the-loop control for autonomous and semiautonomous agents: the agent proposes, a person authorizes, and the tool enforces.
overallExplanation: Enforce the refund threshold in the tool with a required human approval for amounts above $200, rejecting unapproved calls server-side. Prompt emphasis, reviewer models, and temperature settings are all probabilistic where a hard limit is needed.

domain: Plan and manage an Azure AI solution
objective: Implement responsible AI across generative AI and agentic systems
question: A newly deployed operations agent is configured with the full tool set used by the platform team, including a database tool whose managed identity holds Contributor on the data subscription, and it runs unattended overnight. Governance wants the agent constrained so that a misbehaving run cannot damage systems it has no business touching. Which two changes should be made? (Choose two.)
options: Give the agent only the tools its task requires, removing the rest from its definition rather than relying on it to choose sensibly
Scope the tool's managed identity to least privilege, replacing subscription-level Contributor with the narrowest data-plane role on the specific resources it must use
Keep every tool available but add instructions describing which tools the agent should use in which situations
Keep the broad role assignment but enable diagnostic logging so any destructive action is recorded for later review
optionExplanations: Correct. A tool the agent does not have cannot be called under any prompt, injection, or reasoning error, so trimming the tool set is the most reliable constraint available. It also improves tool selection accuracy, because the model chooses among fewer, more relevant options.

Correct. The agent's real blast radius is defined by the permissions of the identity behind its tools, so subscription-wide Contributor means one bad call can affect anything in the subscription. Narrowing to the minimum data-plane role on specific resources bounds the damage independently of agent behaviour.

Instructions guide a probabilistic system and are exactly what governance is asking to stop relying on. Every tool remains callable, so the blast radius is unchanged and an injected or confused run can still reach it.

Logging is a detective control that records destruction after it happens, which for an unattended overnight run means discovery hours later. It belongs in the design, but not as a replacement for reducing permissions.
principle: constrain agents by capability and permission, not by instruction
relatedConcept: Governing agent behaviour combines tool-access controls — which tools exist for this agent — with least-privilege identities behind those tools, so oversight does not depend on the model's judgement.
overallExplanation: Restrict the agent to the tools its task needs and scope the tool identity to least privilege on specific resources. Instructions and after-the-fact logging leave the blast radius of an unattended run unchanged.

domain: Plan and manage an Azure AI solution
objective: Implement responsible AI across generative AI and agentic systems
question: A marketing copy generator is being prepared for external use. Legal raises two concerns: outputs occasionally reproduce long passages that match published copyrighted text, and the assistant sometimes names a competitor brand in comparisons, which brand guidelines forbid. Which combination of platform controls addresses both concerns?
options: Enable protected material detection for text on the deployment and add a custom blocklist containing the prohibited competitor brand terms
Raise the severity thresholds on all four harm categories so more content is blocked, which will catch both the copied passages and the brand names
Add both requirements to the system prompt and instruct the model never to reproduce copyrighted text or mention competitors
Use a groundedness evaluator on each generation and reject any output whose groundedness score falls below a threshold
optionExplanations: Correct. These are two different problems with two matching platform features: protected material detection for text flags completions that match known published content, while a custom blocklist enforces an organization-specific term list such as competitor names. Neither is covered by the standard harm categories, which is why both must be configured explicitly.

The four harm categories cover hate, sexual, violence, and self-harm content, and no threshold setting makes them recognize copyrighted passages or brand names. Raising thresholds would also block more legitimate marketing copy while missing both stated concerns.

System prompt rules are advisory: the model has no reliable way to know which text is copyrighted, and brand mentions slip through in paraphrase or comparison. Legal exposure of this kind needs detection at the response level, not a request in the instructions.

Groundedness measures whether an answer is supported by provided sources, which is unrelated to whether generated text matches copyrighted material or names a competitor. It is the right evaluator for a RAG assistant and the wrong control here.
principle: match each risk to the control built for it
relatedConcept: Content moderation in Foundry extends past the four harm categories to protected material detection and custom blocklists for organization-specific terms.
overallExplanation: Protected material detection for text catches reproduction of copyrighted passages, and a custom blocklist enforces prohibited brand terms. Harm-category thresholds, prompt instructions, and groundedness scoring do not detect either risk.
